data.title: Vance warns US still 'in the middle of the game' with Iran despite talks
data.description:
Vice President Vance said Saturday that the U.S. had made progress in negotiations with Iran but warned the war is still “in the middle of the game” as the Trump administration presses Tehran for concessions to help bring the conflict to an end.

“I do think that we’ve made some progress over the last few days,” Vance told Fox News’ Kayleigh McEnany, pointing to negotiations between Iran and Oman over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

But Vance cautioned against viewing the talks as a sign that an end to the war is imminent.

“This thing is not over. It’s obviously not at the beginning. We’re in the middle of the game,” he said. “We’re applying a whole host of tools, diplomatic, economic, military tools, to ensure that we get the best outcome for the American people.”

Vance’s comments come after Joint Chiefs of Staff Chair Gen. Dan Caine urged top Trump administration officials to find an “off-ramp” from the nearly six-month war with Iran, according to a new report.

Caine raised the prospect of finding a way out of the conflict in conversations with CIA Director John Ratcliffe, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President Vance, CNN reported Friday, citing multiple sources familiar with the discussions.

“Caine is looking for an off ramp,” one source told CNN.

The nation’s top military officer also reportedly warned senior administration officials that continued U.S. airstrikes alone are unlikely to achieve President Trump’s objectives in Iran.

Caine and others privately conceded that bombing Iran is unlikely to force the nation to accept a deal on Trump’s terms, adding to growing concerns among top officials about the military options available to the president.

The discussions came ahead of meetings with Trump in an effort to coordinate their message about the risks and limitations of further military action, including options that would not require deploying U.S. troops on the ground.

data.title: Live updates: Senate hits recess button; Iran signals Hormuz deal close but demands remain
data.description:
Iranian officials signaled Saturday that Iran and Oman are “close” to a final framework on a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, but it will require some concessions from the U.S. and Israel.

Vice President Vance also cast doubt on the speed of potential negotiations, saying the U.S. and Tehran are still in “the middle of the game.”

Senators wrapped up a busy final stretch of work overnight into Saturday, confirming Todd Blanche to lead the Justice Department (DOJ) and passing a stopgap funding bill before adjourning for the August recess.

Meanwhile, Trump is facing fresh questions about the economy heading into the fall. A weaker-than-expected July jobs report on Friday showed employers cutting 23,000 jobs, as rising inflation and affordability dominate voters’ concerns ahead of the midterm elections.

Hunter Biden, the son of former President Biden, also offered a glimpse into his father’s battle with prostate cancer and weighed in on how his pardon could affect the Biden legacy.

Follow live below.

data.title: Hunter Biden commends 'woken up' Massie, Greene for standing up to Trump
data.description:
Hunter Biden, son of former President Joe Biden, stated that he liked the “woken up” version of former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) and Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.). 

In a promo for his appearance on former Fox News host Tucker Carlson’s self-titled show, Biden aired his support of Massie and Greene following their criticism of various Trump administration policies.

“I like Thomas Massie and Marjorie Taylor Greene. I like that there are people that have kind of woken up,” he said.

Massie publicly broke away from Trump several high-profile issues, including the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files, foreign policy and the president’s ballroom renovation.

“He was a bad guy. He deserves to lose,” Trump told reporters at the White House’s annual Congressional Picnic following Massie’s loss to Trump-backed Ed Gallrein in Kentucky’s GOP primaries.

Greene said on conspiracy theorist Alex Jones’s “Infowars” that Trump is “not the same man that we supported” for a decade.

“The American people have to open their eyes and deal with reality and deal with truth. And the truth is, look, you may have supported President Trump for 10 years, like I did and like you have, but this is not the same man,” she continued. 

Greene met with Massie and Carlson, posting on Aug. 1 that she believed Trump had “betrayed us all.”

She teased a potential political movement, writing in the post, “Our commitment is America First for all Americans, right, left, and center. The movement has begun.”

The cracks in the Republican party extended to conservative political commentator Candace Owens, who Biden said he liked in the promotion. She apologized in an interview with Biden for her contributions to public criticism he faced during the 2020 presidential election for his drug addiction and the laptop scandal.

Political analyst Nate Silver said Thursday that President Trump’s approval rating is at a new second-term low in July. The drop in satisfaction with the current administration follows attacks resuming in Iran and rising gas prices across the country, according to Silver.

The full interview between Biden and Carlson will be released on Aug. 10.

data.title: Bessent says K-shaped economy is 'over'
data.description:
(NewsNation) — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the “K-shaped” economy has come to an end, arguing lower-income Americans are beginning to regain ground.

“I can say here definitively, the K-shaped economy is over,” Bessent said in an interview with CNBC’s “Squawk Box” earlier this week.

The letter “K” has become shorthand for the diverging economic fortunes of higher- and lower-income Americans in recent years, reflected in everything from wealth accumulation to spending patterns.

The Treasury chief, however, maintains that the K-shaped era is over and says a “C-economy” is emerging, “where the lower-end of wage earners are finally clawing it back, just like they did in President Trump’s first term.”

To support his argument, the treasury secretary pointed to Bureau of Labor Statistics data showing pay grew faster for lower earners than for higher earners in the second quarter.

The data showed weekly earnings for full-time workers at the 25th percentile rose 5.5 percent from a year earlier, compared with 1.5 percent for those at the 75th percentile.

But Bessent’s figures don’t account for inflation. Consumer prices rose 3.9 percent over the same period, eating into workers’ wage gains.

Stubborn inflation is one reason many consumers remain sour on the economy despite a surging stock market, lower unemployment and larger tax refunds.

In January, annual inflation had cooled to 2.4 percent. But the war in Iran sent shock waves through energy markets, helping accelerate inflation to 4.2 percent in May, its fastest annual pace since 2023.

The spike in gas prices became another example of the “K-shaped” split, as lower-income households cut back on consumption while wealthier households were largely undeterred.

As recently as June, Moody’s Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi declared the K-shaped economy “firmly intact,” arguing that the top 20 percent of the income distribution — those making more than $175,000 a year — continue to drive the economy.

At the same time, the picture has become more nuanced.

“The K-shape persists, but lower-income consumers have increased their spending versus last year,” Mark Matthews, chief economist at the National Retail Federation, wrote in a recent analysis.

Among 6 of the bottom 8 spending deciles, discretionary spending outpaced spending on staples, suggesting consumers “seem to be willing to focus more of their spending on the things they want rather than the things they need,” Matthews added.

Whether that signals the end of the K-shaped economy, as Bessent argues, or simply a less pronounced version of it remains an open question.

Matthews cautioned that “softening wage growth” coupled with “sticky inflation” means the second half of the year may not be as rosy as the first.

If consumer sentiment is any guide, many Americans didn’t find the first half especially rosy either.

data.title: The China shock comes to Africa
data.description:
The China shock has arrived in Africa, and America’s economic relationship with the world’s fastest-growing continent is at stake.

America’s own China shock is well documented. Beijing’s entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001 lowered economic barriers. This unleashed a wave of cheap manufactured exports that hollowed out American factory towns and led multiple administrations to impose escalating tariffs on Chinese goods.

The aftershock is now spreading. The same dumping dynamic — Chinese goods exported at below production costs — that shook America’s industrial Midwest, is hitting home in Europe, Latin America, Southeast Asia, and above all, Africa. Chinese import penetration there is rising faster than anywhere else on earth. Across the continent’s major markets — Egypt, Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa — Chinese goods are capturing market share in textiles, steel, autos, machinery, and electronics, and the effect is evident. Manufacturing’s share of GDP across much of Sub-Saharan Africa has stagnated at under 13 percent as Chinese import shares climb.

In contrast to what happened in the United States, where Chinese goods caused labor market shocks in specific geographies, subsidized Chinese exports are killing African manufacturing in the crib. Local industries are being denied the opportunity to scale up and provide the middle-class job opportunities the population needs, and the timing could hardly be worse. By 2040, Africa’s working-age population is projected to exceed that of India and China combined, and finding opportunities for those workers will be Africa’s primary security challenge for years to come.

So why hasn’t Africa protected itself? Partly because there’s less to defend — Africa doesn’t have a major industrial constituency demanding protection. But the bigger constraint is debt vulnerability. Beijing is Africa’s largest creditor, and that debt dependency limits both the fiscal space for subsidies for homegrown industry and the political room for tariffs. You cannot easily impose tariffs on the same country that is restructuring your loans or financing your ports and railways. Moreover, because African economies are relatively small on their own, no single head of state will want to confront China for fear of facing retaliation on their own.

The African Continental Free Trade Area offers a way around that asymmetry. Acting as a bloc rather than 50 separate economies, African governments could harmonize external tariffs, coordinate infant-industry protections across borders, and create a regional market large enough to make local manufacturing genuinely viable. Scale and unity are what can give Africa more space to push back against Beijing on both debt dependency and dumping.

Chinese goods flooding Africa is also an American problem: If Chinese goods continue to flood African markets, American exporters and local industry alike will be crowded out, too. A key starting point is greater U.S. engagement with the free trade area.

It is imperative that Washington gets it right, since whoever shapes the bloc’s rules will hold significant power over who gets to sell into that market. China has already moved to fill that role: it has positioned itself as a leading technical partner to Africa, advising on the bloc’s rules for intellectual property rights, investment, competition policy and digital trade. The United States needs to get its own advisers into those technical discussions. The State Department should use the newly announced U.S.-Africa Strategic Investment Program to fund this as quickly as possible.

None of this will work, though, without decoupling debt structuring from continued dependence on opaque China-linked infrastructure financing. African finance ministers need alternative lenders and refinancing mechanisms that don’t come bundled with commitments to Chinese contractors and equipment. One problem is that the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation — America’s largest development finance entity — has grown so narrowly focused on critical minerals and national security that it is missing opportunities to advance America’s long-term economic security in Africa.

The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation needs a mandate to innovate: to design new instruments that pull passive, return-seeking American capital into African infrastructure at real scale. U.S. mutual funds and exchange-traded funds alone held nearly $45 trillion in assets — even a sliver of that pool would close Africa’s infrastructure financing gap. This administration, stocked with veterans of Wall Street and the capital markets, is well placed to build that kind of bridge — if it chooses to point that expertise at Africa.

The first China shock reshaped America’s politics, economics, and even society. Its aftershocks will determine Africa’s economic future.

Daniel Swift is a senior research analyst for economics, finance, and trade for the Center on Economic and Financial Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, where Cameron Timlin is an intern. Swift is a retired U.S. diplomat and was mostly recently the Acting Coordinator for Prosper Africa.

data.title: Why pink seems to be the 'in' color of 2026, years after 'Barbie'
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – Every year, there’s a new trend that takes over the cultural zeitgeist. The “trad wife” trend, your kids saying 6-7, making sourdough and the sensation of “Barbenheimer,” are among the most recent.

As fads do, they eventually fade. Some, like jorts and landline phones, have returned. 

There’s another trend that we cannot seem to get away from: the color pink. 

A few summers ago, amidst Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour and the release of the “Barbie” movie, seeing pink everywhere made sense. The color was prominent in both highly attended entertainment events.

But pink wasn’t forecasted to be the color of 2026; Pantone bestowed that title upon “cloud dancer.”

Nonetheless, pink has shown through.

There were bright pink cleats galore at the World Cup, and WNBA star Angel Reese is releasing a new pink basketball shoe. Starbucks and Dunkin have released pink drinks. Farmers Insurance recently launched a soft-pink rebrand. A$AP Rocky made waves with a pink Chanel diaper bag in spring.

Experts aren’t entirely surprised, either. As Lizzo sings, it “goes with everything.”

“It really is a great color from the science point,” said Rachel Plybon Beach, a teaching assistant professor and program coordinator for interior architecture at the School of Art and Design at West Virginia University’s College of Creative Arts and Media. “The hues are really broad, so you can go from warm to cool, and they can play with it.”

You could use pink as a dominant color, more subtly in the background, or as a pop through an accessory. It works well with lighting in your home and, in fashion, it can complement your complexion and prove to be very flattering.

Pink’s versatility makes it attractive not only in fashion, textiles, apparel and architecture, but to psychologists and marketers. 

“Don’t think for a second they didn’t know [pink] would be popular after ‘Barbie,’” Plybon Beach told Nexstar. “They knew, and they knew the exact kind of pink to appeal to people.” 

Our brains may view pink as calming or denoting transition, studies have suggested. This could be from the importance of sunrises and sunsets to our ancestors, which helped them move into or out of their higher-activity days. Other theories argue lighter shades of pink could be among our first sensory memories stretching back to the womb. 

A very specific shade of pink, dubbed Baker-Miller pink, was found to calm prisoners, youth in a detention center, and psychiatric patients. Another study linked pink with a sense of optimism.

In the case of Swift’s “Eras Tour,” Plybon Beach argues the color fit the mood. The shows were meant to be fun, happy and inviting, a vibe pink hues can easily create. A similar connection could be seen with pink’s appearance in the World Cup, in which cultures from around the world came together. 

It also pairs well with other colors that have been trending recently, including neutrals like warm beige, light blues and greens, and whites and grays.

Society’s influence on trending colors

Pink hasn’t always been so dominant. Roughly three decades ago, pink was very “in” in the land of fashion, Colleen Moretz, an associate professor of fashion design and merchandising and head of the Fashion Design Studios, also at the School of Art and Design, recalled. 

“And then it faded, and then pink was like, too cute,” Moretz explained to Nexstar. Its comeback is present, though, especially among the younger generation. 

Sometimes colors shine because of a cultural moment. After the Sept. 11 attacks, red, white and blue were everywhere, Moretz said. They’re back again now, thanks to America’s semiquincentennial. 

During the COVID-19 pandemic, when many found themselves at home more, there was a shift toward more comfortable clothing. Because athleisure wear primarily comes in neutral colors, those shades of whites and grays became more prevalent, Moretz explained. 

Pink had its own similar moment during the Great Depression, standing as one of the few colors of lipsticks and blush that Americans could afford at the time. The color could bring cheer to the wearer in an otherwise troubling time.

“Right now, I think we need a little bit of happiness,” Plybon Beach said in regard to pink’s current popularity.

Where you come in

Psychology, history and science aside, there’s another factor that fuels a color’s prominence: consumers. 

“If the consumer likes it and they start buying it … we start shifting gears,” Plybon Beach explained. “‘Oh, that’s what they want right now? That’s what we’ll do.’”

If you want to get in on a color trend, but aren’t ready to fully commit, Plybon Beach and Moretz recommend looking at accents. Think artwork, lampshades, throw pillows, or an area rug in your home, and jewelry, makeup, scarves, shoes, or a purse in your outfit. 

“You don’t have to go all out, but you can add … different elements of that color without going, you know, all out,” Moretz said. 

And if you want to get ahead of the color trends, you may only need to consider a scene from “The Devil Wears Prada,” specifically Meryl Streep’s remarks on Anne Hathaway’s cerulean sweater. 

Couture lines and fashion houses — as Streep, playing Miranda Priestly, suggested — are often the first to spark the use of certain colors and fabrics in clothing. Interiors then tend to follow suit, Plybon Beach said. 

The next colors that could break through? Yellow and oranges, according to Moretz and Plybon Beach. A rise in interest in a Western theme, potentially fueled by “Yellowstone,” may drive other colors to the forefront as well. 

But it will ultimately come down to consumers as to whether it balloons in popularity. 

That can be further divided by the age of consumers. Those on the younger side may be “more willing to go over the edge a little bit,” while those who are older are “looking at it as more of an investment.” 

“I always talk about costs per wear,” Moretz explained. If you feel you won’t wear a yellow top very much, for example, it may feel more expensive than, say, a pink top you’re going to wear more frequently. The same concept is true in interiors, where it’s known as life cycle cost. 

Trending colors, like shag carpets and straight-leg jeans, are cyclical. If the shades of pinks, yellows and oranges that are growing now don’t fit your preferences, you may only need to wait until a new hue rises to the top.

data.title: Congress debates childhood by budget lines. Children don't live that way.
data.description:
Direct investments in children are among the most effective and highest-return policies the government runs. Yet America already spends less on children than many wealthy peer nations and less per child than per senior. And now Congress is weighing another round of choices that would further reshape the systems supporting children through school, healthcare, nutrition, childcare and housing.

Some of those choices are already law. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that the 2025 reconciliation law will reduce federal spending on SNAP benefits by over $250 billion over the 2025-2034 period.

Others remain as proposals. The House Appropriations Committee-approved fiscal 2027 transportation and housing bill carries a total discretionary allocation that’s 10.4 percent below the fiscal 2026 enacted level. President Trump’s budget requests a reduction of $10.7 billion or 13 percent for the Department of Housing and Urban Development. The House committee’s labor and health bill proposes increases of just $10 million each for Head Start and the Child Care and Development Block Grant.

The federal spending debate usually begins with cost: What can the country afford, what should families provide themselves and what role should the government play? Our recent study in Nature Communications points to a prior question: Do lawmakers know where public support already narrows inequality and where families are largely on their own?

We combined public spending, family expenditures and caregivers’ time to estimate what America invests in children from birth through age 18 across education, healthcare, nutrition, housing, childcare, transportation and clothing. The result is a kind of MRI of childhood, captured before the latest proposals take effect.

It shows that gaps open well before children reach public school. By age 5, the cumulative investment gap between children in the highest and lowest income families exceeds $40,000, out of roughly $500,000 a typical child receives across childhood.

The largest driver is housing. Housing accounts for about one-third of the income — and race-based — investment gaps we measure. Yet fewer than 4 percent of U.S. households with children receive housing assistance. Even among families in the bottom income quartile, only about 13 percent receive support. That is not a marginal gap in a niche program. It is a central hole in the childhood safety net.

Housing pressures remain widespread. Census data show that nearly half of renter households spend more than 30 percent of their income on housing. Direct housing assistance for families with children, meanwhile, remains rare.

Childcare presents a similar problem. We find that Black and Hispanic children receive about 40 percent less investment in formal childcare than white children, while income-based gaps approach 70 percent. The national average annual price of childcare was $13,184 in 2025. When public support is thin and prices are high, access increasingly depends on family resources.

Families also fill gaps with time. The largest yearly investment we measure for any child is not tuition, rent or childcare. It is parents’ and caregivers’ time during the first months of life feeding and taking care of infants, worth nearly $20,000 in forgone wages. But even time is unequal. Low-income infants receive less than higher-income peers, a pattern consistent with who can afford leave from work. The United States remains the only Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development country without paid maternity leave at the national level.

Public schools and Medicaid show the opposite lesson. When the government commits to broad access, total investment gaps shrink. At kindergarten entry, schooling investments are far more equal than investments in housing or childcare. Medicaid likewise offsets healthcare inequalities that would otherwise be larger.

But equal totals do not erase inequality. The same dollar often buys different experiences. Lower-income, Black and Hispanic children are more likely to receive emergency room care, tutoring and special education — services often designed to respond after problems appear. Higher-income children are more likely to receive scheduled pediatric visits and enrichment through music lessons, sports and museum visits. A dollar spent catching up is not the same as a dollar spent getting ahead.

That is why the current budget debate is too fragmented. A cut to housing assistance is treated as housing policy. A reduction in childcare support is treated as childcare policy. A change to nutrition benefits is treated as food policy. But children do not grow up in budget silos. Their lives are shaped by the combination of a home, healthcare, food, childcare, schools and the time adults can afford to spend with them.

Reasonable people can disagree about the size of the government. But if lawmakers choose to spend less on children, they should do so with a clear map of where public support already narrows inequality and where the safety net is threadbare.

David Blazar and Michel Boudreaux are the lead authors of the study, “Disparities in childhood human capital investments in the United States,” which was supported by the Spencer Foundation. Blazar is the Malen Professor for Urban Education Policy at the University of Maryland, College Park and Boudreaux is an associate professor of health policy and management at the University of Maryland, College Park.

data.title: Hunter Biden says Joe Biden's cancer is spreading: 'It's very debilitating'
data.description:
Former President Joe Biden’s cancer has spread to other parts of his body, his son Hunter Biden revealed in an interview, describing the disease as “very painful” and “very debilitating.”

“The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further,” he told the BBC’s “Newsnight” Friday. “It’s really sad to watch.”

Several months after leaving the White House, the former president announced in May 2025 that he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer. At the time, his office said the cancer appeared to be “hormone-sensitive,” allowing for “effective management.”

Hunter Biden became emotional during the interview while discussing his father’s condition, saying that watching the former president’s health decline has been “really hard.”

“The only thing that I’d say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good,” he said.

Despite the cancer’s progression, Hunter Biden said his 83-year-old father remains active and engaged in public life.

Former first lady Jill Biden said in a June “The View” appearance that, while things have “slowed down” for her husband since his diagnosis, he is still keeping busy.

Aside from a memoir slated to come out around the November midterm elections — and a late July controversy surrounding leaked audio files appearing to show the former president sharing classified information with a ghostwriter in 2016 and 2017 — former President Biden seldom weighs in on the current political landscape.

In June, however, he delivered a speech a Democratic Party Gala in Maryland — swiping at President Trump’s multiple Washington D.C. renovation projects.

“It’s not just his vanity projects … putting his name on the Kennedy Center. Building an arch in his own honor. Even hiring his own pool guy to fix the reflecting pool,” the former president said. “Whoa, what a loser.”

“He’s still doing his thing,” Hunter Biden said during Friday’s BBC interview. “He so believes in this country.”

Hunter Biden also reflected on his father’s infamous June 2024 debate performance against President Trump, saying he felt “shocked” while watching from home in California.

“I knew something was wrong,” he said of the debate.

Hunter Biden said his father remains at the “center of our family” as he undergoes treatment, calling the former president the “best father, the best husband, the best grandfather.”

data.title: Maher says Trump further left than Dems citing Intel stake: 'This is socialism'
data.description:
Comedian Bill Maher accused President Trump of openly embracing “socialism” more than Democrats, as democratic socialism is on the rise in the U.S.

In a Friday segment on “Real Time,” Maher said Republicans were hypocrites when it came to accusing democratic socialists of being communist, especially the Trump administration.

“It’s so interesting, the wrinkle in this story, because now that they’re communists, there’s an opening for socialism. And you know who’s filling it? Donald Trump,” he said. 

Maher called out the Trump administration’s stake in Intel, Nvidia and Nippon Steel, saying “we basically run their boardroom now.”

Trump said in April that federal stock holdings in Intel generated more than $30 billion over the last several months, after he authorized the U.S. government’s investment in the struggling semiconductor chip manufacturing company last summer.

“It’s like, what? The president is just singling out a huge CEO of an important company and so they had to scramble the Jets and have a meeting at the White House and what happened at the end of that meeting? Okay, you say we get 10% of your company. That is thuggish behavior,” Maher said.

The decision garnered support from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) but drew pushback from Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) called it a “terrible idea” and a “step toward socialism.”

“If socialism is government owning the means of production, wouldn’t the government owning part of Intel be step toward socialism?” he wrote on social media.

“And you know this is socialism, I think, because Bernie Sanders agrees with it all. He wants to do it with the AI companies,” Maher continued.

Trump has likened democratic socialism to communism in remarks made to reporters in the Oval Office in June. 

Candidates affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) have been winning elections across the country.

“I think it’s the biggest threat to our nation there is, maybe since our founding,” he continued. “That includes World War I, World War II, September 11, it includes the Pearl Harbor attack.”

“We have never seen anything like this in modern time,” Maher concluded about Trump’s government stake.

data.title: Miller saga muddles midterm landscape for Ohio GOP
data.description:
The controversy around Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) is complicating the midterm landscape for Ohio Republicans as Democrats build momentum in the Buckeye State, a former battleground that’s become a red state in the Trump era.

Miller, who is running for a third term in a competitive House district, is facing calls to step down after allegations of domestic abuse toward his ex-wife, the daughter of Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). He has forcefully denied the claims, but the controversy could make his red seat an easier pick-up opportunity for Democrats in the high-stakes fight for House control. 

Ohio is also host to a highly competitive Senate race, where former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) has lodged a comeback bid against incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R) that could bolster Democrats’ chances of taking back the upper chamber this fall — plus a neck-and-neck race for Ohio governor in the state that’s been GOP-led for more than a decade.  

“In an environment where Republicans have been particularly strong in Ohio, this year’s environment is going to be much more challenging for them, and this certainly doesn’t help things,” said Robert Alexander, a political science professor at Bowling Green State University in Ohio, on the Miller developments. 

“I think that the fact that so much of the attention is on Republicans is a good thing for Democrats,” he added. “The more it’s about Republicans, I think the better that Democrats will likely do.”

Miller has denied allegations from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, in a New York Times report last week that the Ohio lawmaker scalded her chest with hot water, held a gun to her head and fractured their daughter’s collarbone, among other allegations. The pair divorced in 2025 and have since been locked in a bitter custody battle over their daughter. 

The House Ethics Committee announced Monday that it’s investigating allegations of domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use after Miller said he has “nothing to hide.” 

Miller also said that he received a Monday phone call from President Trump, who told him that it would be a tough race and that he didn’t know whether the embattled lawmaker would be able to pull it off in the fall. The House Republican said he drew comparisons to the president’s own controversies on the 2016 campaign trail, signaling his intent to stay in the race. 

But a new co/efficient polling memo released this week showed Miller down 14 percentage points against Brook Park City Council member Brian Poindexter, the Democrat nominee for the typically red 7th Congressional District. 

“The district is Republican, but it’s not so heavily Republican that a Democrat could never win,” said Justin Buchler, an associate professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland.

Now, a chorus of Capitol Hill Republicans are calling for Miller to resign ahead of an Aug. 10 deadline that would let the state GOP pick a replacement nominee for the November ballot. 

Bernie Moreno, the senator and Miller’s former father-in-law, said the congressman needs “serious psychological help.” Husted, in the middle of his must-win Senate fight, said Miller needs to “step aside as a candidate” and resign.

Democrats are also signaling that the Miller controversy could become a liability for the GOP in other House races.

“Every single vulnerable Republican who has coddled and stood by these creeps should be ashamed of themselves,” Democrats’ House campaign arm spokesperson Viet Shelton said in a statement.

Mehek Cooke, an Ohio Republican strategist, told The Hill that Miller has become “an unnecessary distraction” as Republicans head into a highly competitive midterm year. She shrugged off the latest polling, but called for Miller to step aside. 

“Republicans should take this race seriously [and] put forward candidates who reflect our values and keep the focus on delivering results,” Cooke wrote in an email. 

Buchler drew parallels to the controversy that built around Democrat Graham Platner’s Senate bid in Maine until the progressive bowed to calls from party leaders to withdraw. 

“There came a point at which it was just too much,” Buchler said of the pressure on Platner. 

If Miller does stay in the race, “then you have a candidate who is, in some ways, damaged by the allegations, and in some ways damaged by political leaders in the state coming out against him,” Buchler said. “If he does step down, then you have the question of who fills the vacancy.” 

In response to an inquiry about the Miller saga, House Republicans campaign arm’s spokesperson Zach Bannon projected confidence without directly namedropping the embattled lawmaker. 

“Ohio’s 7th congressional district is a Republican seat that strongly backed President Trump and consistently rejects the radical left’s agenda. It will remain red this November,” Bannon said. 

As the Miller saga unfolds, the stage is set for highly competitive races for the Senate and governor’s mansion that could mean Democrats gain ground in the red state. Once considered a purple national bellwether, Ohio has grown increasingly red since siding with Trump in each of his three presidential elections — but experts say that could change. 

“Ohio leans Republican, but it is not a solidly Republican Deep South state,” Buchler said. “This is a midterm, which means that elections nationwide are going to move towards the party out of the White House, that’s the Democrats. That could, in principle, mean that Democrats pick up some wins in states like Ohio.” 

Brown, a major recruit for Democrats, has pulled slightly ahead of Husted in Decision Desk HQ’s (DDHQ) polling average of the Senate race, which prognosticators consider among just a handful of toss-up contests that could determine the upper chamber’s majority.

Term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine (R) last year appointed Husted, then the lieutenant governor, to temporarily fill Vice President Vance’s old seat in the Senate. The Senate contest is a special election to fill out the remainder of Vance’s term, which runs through 2028. 

In the governor’s race, DeWine has endorsed Vivek Ramaswamy, a biotech entrepreneur and former co-leader at Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), to succeed him. But Ramaswamy lacks elected experience and, as a first-generation American, faces headwinds from some anti-immigrant voters in the GOP.

He faces a tough rival this fall in Democrat Amy Acton, a former Ohio health director who worked with DeWine during the pandemic. Cook Political Report last month shifted the governor’s race toward Democrats, into the toss-up column. 

“It is a coin flip for both the governor’s race and the Senate race. I wouldn’t be surprised if both of those races were within the margin of error, ultimately,” Alexander said. 

At the same time, Ohio is also home to a handful of competitive House races that could give Republicans new pickup opportunities under newly redrawn, GOP-friendly maps.

Democratic Reps. Marcy Kaptur and Greg Landsman are both running in reshaped districts, Cook rates as “toss up” and “lean Democrat” contests, respectively. 

Ohio GOP consultant Matt Dole attributed the Rust Belt state’s highly competitive environment in part to Trump fatigue — as the president weathers lackluster approval ratings, and frustration over his handling of the economy and the war in Iran — and to a “general fatigue” with Republicans in a state where the party has dominated every statewide partisan office since 2010. 

Republicans are still feeling bullish about their midterm chances this cycle, Dole said, “but it is certainly the most competitive we’ve seen in the last 20 years.”
